impact: Letlow was endorsed by Gov. Landry and Trump, so a win puts a Landry ally in the Senate seat; federal levers (Title I, ESSER successors, TANF reauthorization) flow into the LA district budgets that buy Star.
result_note: Incumbent Bill Cassidy (R) finished third in the closed GOP primary and is not on the ballot; Letlow beat John Fleming in the June 27 GOP runoff. An Independent (Jamie LaBranche) appears on one Ballotpedia page: unverified. Rated Solid/Safe R. No results reported at time of research.

office: Constitutional Amendment 2: local property tax millage rates after reassessment
impact: Rules on rolling millages forward after reassessment directly affect local school district property tax revenue, which funds district purchases such as Star Academy sites.
result_note: One of 10 amendments on the Nov 3 ballot. Amendment number and exact text per Invest in Louisiana table; verify against SOS/PAR guide.

office: Constitutional Amendment (reported as No. 5): order of paying down retirement system unfunded liabilities (HB 27)
impact: Lets state retirement systems apply nonrecurring money to any unfunded liability; how TRSL debt is paid down shapes district employer contribution rates and freed-up district dollars.
result_note: Amendment number unverified across sources. Separate from the May 2026 teacher-pay Amendment 3, which voters rejected (~58% no).

office: Constitutional Amendment 4: governor lifetime term limit (two terms for life)
impact: Changes gubernatorial term limits from two consecutive terms to a lifetime cap; relevant to the long-run horizon of the Landry relationship.
result_note: Other Nov 3 amendments cover disabled-veteran tax exemption transfer (1), no bail after conviction for aggravated offenses against minors (3), drinking water service lines, foreign-adversary expropriation (8), blighted property tax exemption (10). A Ballotpedia page showing a 63.43% result appears erroneous/stale; treat as unreported.

office: U.S. House LA-2 (New Orleans; open all-party primary)
candidates: Troy Carter (D, inc.); Peter Williams (R); Lisa Ballay (L); Renada "Honey" Collins (I)
impact: Covers Orleans Parish, home of NOLA Education HQ and Orleans Star sites; Carter is the federal point of contact for New Orleans education funding.
result_note: After SCOTUS struck the prior map, Landry signed a new map May 29, 2026; May/June House primaries were canceled and House races moved to a Nov 3 open primary with Dec 12 runoff. Challenger list is inconsistent across sources (Collins listed as D in one source; Walter 'Rocky' Beach (I) in another): non-incumbent names partly unverified.

office: U.S. House LA-6 (Baton Rouge area; open seat, open primary)
candidates: Rick Edmonds (R); Blake Miguez (R); Lindsay "Rubia" Garcia (D)
impact: Open Baton Rouge seat after Cleo Fields (D) declined to run under the new map; Edmonds is a former state lawmaker on education issues and Miguez is a Landry-aligned state senator.
result_note: 10 candidates (6 R, 3 D, 1 L). Likely heads to Dec 12 runoff. Other candidates unverified. Miguez residency dispute (AG says primary residence New Iberia).

office: U.S. House runoffs (any LA district with no majority on Nov 3)
impact: Second round for open-primary House races under the new map; also the runoff date for any local Nov 3 contests.
result_note: Matchups depend on tonight's results.

office: Orleans / Caddo school board or school millage items
impact: No Orleans or Caddo school millage found on Nov 3; Caddo renewed three school millages in March 2025 and Orleans renewed its facilities millage in 2025, so Star host-district local revenue looks stable.
result_note: Unverified: no sample-ballot confirmation. Some other parishes (e.g., St. Charles, Sabine) have school millage renewals listed for 2026; check SOS for each Star host parish.

impact: Star's 50-site LA footprint and its Landry relationship ride on this race; the governor drives the budget, BESE appointees, and the MFP that funds districts.
result_note: Landry is eligible for a second term but has not announced (as of sources found). No 2027 field verified. Date per Wikipedia listing; unverified against SOS. Governor races remain jungle primary.

office: Board of Elementary and Secondary Education (8 elected seats)
impact: BESE sets MFP formula, accountability, and appoints the State Superintendent (Cade Brumley), so it directly controls K-12 policy and funding Star depends on.
result_note: Candidates unverified; no 2026-dated source found on 2027 BESE races. BESE moves to closed party primaries under the 2024 law; exact 2027 dates unverified.

impact: Limited education role; included for completeness of the 2027 statewide slate.
result_note: Candidates unverified.

candidates: Cindy Hyde-Smith (R, inc.); Scott Colom (D); Ty Pinkins (I)
impact: Federal education and TANF appropriations; Hyde-Smith sits on Appropriations.
result_note: Rated Solid/Safe R (Silver Bulletin, Split Ticket, Oct 31); some observers see a possible Colom upset.

office: Mississippi House special elections (two seats, formerly Reps. Price Wallace and Bo Brown)
impact: Minor effect on House supermajority math for education budget votes.
result_note: District numbers and candidates unverified.

office: County school boards and municipal separate school district trustees
impact: Local boards approve district program contracts; relevant wherever Star has or targets MS sites.
result_note: On Nov 3 ballot statewide (qualifying closed Aug 20, 2026). Individual candidates unverified; e.g., Scott County School Board District 2 special.

impact: No education measure identified.
result_note: No verified statewide measure on the Nov 3 ballot; HCR 26 (reproductive rights) status unverified. Initiative process inoperable since 2021.

candidates: Andy Gipson (R); Philip Gunn (R); Lynn Fitch (R); Priscilla Till (other)
impact: Next governor controls MDHS (TANF) and the education budget; MS TANF oversight has been tightened since the welfare scandal, which shapes any TANF-funded program pitch.
result_note: Primaries August 2027. Till's party unverified. Possible: Delbert Hosemann, Shad White, Gregg Harper, Tommy Duff (unverified). No Democrat declared as of Aug 2026. General date is the standard Nov 2, 2027 (unverified).

impact: MS Lt. Gov. runs the Senate and is central to K-12 appropriations.
result_note: Watson (current SOS) announced. Rest of field unverified. State Superintendent is appointed by the State Board, not elected.

impact: Governor proposes the Education Trust Fund budget and is president of the State Board of Education.
result_note: Oct 16-17 poll: Tuberville 51, Jones 40. Rated Solid R.

impact: Presides over the Senate and shapes ETF appropriations committees.
result_note: Wahl beat SOS Wes Allen in June 16 GOP runoff.

impact: Federal education and workforce funding.
result_note: Moore (Trump-endorsed) beat Jared Hudson in June 16 runoff; AG Steve Marshall finished third. Rated Solid R.

impact: SBOE appoints the State Superintendent and sets K-12 policy, including at-risk and dropout-prevention priorities.
result_note: West unopposed in GOP primary. McCurry party per one report; lightly verified.

impact: SBOE seat; incumbent returning unopposed keeps continuity.
result_note: Unopposed in primary and general per available sources.

impact: Incumbent Marie Manning was ousted in the GOP primary, so this seat will change hands and may shift board votes on superintendent and programs.
result_note: Bradford 54% to Manning in May 19 primary (unofficial).

office: State Board of Education District 8 (open; Wayne Reynolds retiring)
impact: Open north Alabama seat; Jones (Moms for Liberty Madison County founder) would shift board composition.
result_note: Jones beat William Matthews 53.6% to 46.4% in June 16 runoff.

office: Statewide Amendment 2: process to consolidate county school boards into multi-county boards
impact: Would create a path for county districts to merge (with SBOE impact study and local referendum), which could change the buyer map for Star contracts in rural Alabama.

office: Statewide Amendment 3: daily Pledge of Allegiance and student-led prayer policies in K-12
impact: School-climate policy mandate; no funding effect.

office: Statewide Amendment 4: weekly Star-Spangled Banner broadcast in K-12
impact: School-day mandate; no funding effect.
Not education-related.
result_note: Details unverified.

office: Mobile County local races (school board, if any)
impact: Mobile County Public Schools hosts Star; local board seats would affect renewals.
result_note: Unverified: no Mobile County school board race on Nov 3 found. Mobile is in SBOE District 1, which is not up in 2026.

impact: Next governor controls TN DHS, which holds a large TANF reserve and grant programs, plus the TISA education funding formula.
result_note: Blackburn heavily favored (Solid R; Aug poll 55-34). If Blackburn wins, she would vacate her U.S. Senate seat and the new governor appoints a replacement. Commissioner of Education is appointed, Lt. Gov. is chosen by the Senate.

impact: Federal education and TANF appropriations.
result_note: Rematch of 2020. A Federalist-line candidate (Andrew Mixon) appears on one Ballotpedia page: unverified.

office: Three constitutional amendments: crime victims' rights, pretrial bail denial, permanent ban on state property tax
impact: No direct K-12 funding effect; property tax ban concerns a state-level tax TN does not levy, local school property taxes unaffected.
result_note: Each needs a majority of votes cast for governor to pass.

office: Haywood County school board / county offices
impact: Haywood County Schools hosts Star; board composition affects renewal.
result_note: TN county general election was Aug 6, 2026 (already held). Whether school board seats were on the ballot and who won is unverified; check haywoodvotes.com results PDF.

office: No general election in 2026 (next: Governor, Legislature, Resident Commissioner)
impact: No 2026 vote affects the Department of the Family contract; current administration stays in place through 2028.
result_note: Puerto Rico holds general elections every four years (last Nov 2024). No 2026 plebiscite or referendum found. 2028 date assumed per standard calendar, unverified.

impact: The superintendent runs the SC Department of Education, which steers at-risk and dropout-prevention priorities and state K-12 dollars that flow to districts hosting Star sites. Weaver is a school-choice advocate; Wright beat Lisa Ellis in the June Democratic primary.
result_note: No general election results found as of search time.

impact: The next governor writes the executive budget and sets K-12 and workforce priorities for the state that funds SC districts' program purchases. Wilson (current Attorney General) won the June 23 GOP runoff over Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette.
result_note: Race rated Solid R by MultiState. No results found yet.

office: Lieutenant Governor (elected on ticket with governor)
impact: Elected jointly with the governor; limited direct role in K-12 funding.
result_note: Running mates per July 2026 reporting (Reichenbach named by Wilson in January 2026).

impact: Federal votes on Title I, ESSER-successor and TANF reauthorization affect district budgets. Darline Graham was appointed July 13, 2026 after Sen. Lindsey Graham died July 11, then won the Aug 25 GOP runoff over Rep. Ralph Norman.
result_note: An Aug Impact Research poll had Andrews 42, Graham 39. Incumbent flag reflects appointed status.

impact: The House originates the state budget, including K-12 appropriations. Pre-election split about 89 R, 35 D; Democrats filed in all 124 districts; rated Safe R. The SC Senate is not up in 2026.
result_note: Control change unlikely per Sabato rating.

impact: No statewide constitutional questions appear on the SC 2026 ballot per one voter guide, so no statewide education funding measure. Local school questions may exist but were not verified for Star host districts (SC host districts not identified).
result_note: Single-source finding (Decode the Vote); unverified against scVOTES.

candidates: Sarah Huckabee Sanders (R, inc.); Fredrick Love (D); Colt Shelby (L)
impact: Sanders' LEARNS Act agenda and executive budget shape funding for Arkansas's 14 Star sites and the state education department that oversees them. Libertarian candidate from a single source.
result_note: Rated Solid R. Arkansas general-election runoffs, if needed, are Dec 1.

impact: Presides over the state Senate; indirect influence on education appropriations. No Democrat filed.

candidates: Tom Cotton (R, inc.); Hallie Shoffner (D); Jeff Wadlin (L)
impact: Federal education and TANF policy votes. Polling conflicted (one Talk Business poll had Shoffner ahead within margin; another report had Cotton up 16).

office: Arkansas General Assembly (all 100 House seats, about 17-18 Senate seats)
impact: The legislature sets school foundation funding and enhanced student achievement (poverty) funding that Arkansas districts use for programs like Star. Republicans hold a three-quarters supermajority needed for most budget bills; Democrats would need to flip about 3 Senate and 6 House seats to break it.
result_note: Runoffs, if any, Dec 1, 2026.

office: Statewide ballot issues (Issue 1 citizens-only voting, Issue 2 right to bear arms, economic development districts amendment, Issue 4 $500M water bonds)
impact: No education-specific statewide measure verified. The economic development districts amendment could affect local property tax capture that funds schools; impact unverified.
result_note: Issue number for the economic development districts amendment unverified.

office: School millage / board elections in Star host districts (Pine Bluff, Helena-West Helena, Stuttgart, Camden Fairview, Strong)
impact: Arkansas districts may hold board and millage votes in spring or November. No November 2026 millage question verified for any Star host district.
result_note: unverified

candidates: Scott Fitzpatrick (R, inc.); Quentin Wilson (D); Dustin Coffell (L)
impact: Only statewide office on Missouri's 2026 ballot; the auditor audits state budget and school district spending. No governor, superintendent (appointed commissioner) or US Senate race in Missouri in 2026.

office: Missouri General Assembly (all 163 House seats, 17 Senate seats)
impact: The legislature sets the school foundation formula and any appropriation that could fund Sikeston's Star program. Democrats need about 3 House and 2 Senate seats to break GOP supermajorities.
result_note: Seat counts vary by source.

office: Amendment 3 (abortion ban with exceptions, repeal of 2024 amendment; minors gender-transition procedures)
impact: No direct education funding effect; drives turnout that could shape legislative races.

office: Amendment 6 (limits on lawmakers rewriting voter-approved measures)
impact: Affects whether future citizen initiatives (including any on school funding or vouchers) can be altered by the legislature.

office: Amendment 7 (Show-Me Prosperity Fund endowment aimed at ending most state taxes over about 100 years)
impact: Long-term state revenue structure change; could eventually affect general revenue available for K-12.

office: Amendment 8 (county sheriffs) and Proposition A (referendum on 2025 congressional map)
impact: No education impact.

office: Sikeston R-6 school district ballot question
impact: Sikeston R-6 voters approved a no-tax-increase bond (Phase 4) in April 2026; Missouri school board and levy votes normally occur in April. No November 2026 Sikeston school question verified.
result_note: unverified for Nov 3; April 2026 bond passed.

office: WV Legislature (all 100 House of Delegates seats, about 17-19 Senate seats incl. 2 specials)
impact: The legislature appropriates TANF and education dollars, including the proposed TANF-funded Star Academy expansion. The size and makeup of the GOP supermajority (about 90-9 House, 32-2 Senate) will shape oversight of that funding.
result_note: Governor not on ballot until 2028. Watch SD13 (Oliverio R vs Williams D) and SD9 (Roberts R vs Antolini).

candidates: Shelley Moore Capito (R, inc.); Rachel Fetty Anderson (D)
impact: Capito sits on Appropriations and influences federal TANF and education funding that WV has tapped for Star Academy. Rated Solid R.
result_note: Capito won the May primary with 66.5 percent over state Sen. Tom Willis and others.

impact: No education impact; the only verified statewide amendment. A homestead exemption increase amendment did not make the ballot.

office: School levies in Star host counties (Logan, Berkeley/Martinsburg, Barbour/Philippi)
impact: Berkeley County voters approved a $115M school bond levy in the May 2026 primary (new middle school and CTE center). No November levy verified for Logan or Barbour. WV state superintendent and board of education are appointed, not elected.
result_note: May 2026 primary result, not Nov 3.

impact: The superintendent runs the Arizona Department of Education, which administers state aid and federal Title I pass-through to charters like Career Success Schools. Yee (state treasurer) ousted incumbent Tom Horne in the July 21 GOP primary; vouchers (ESA) were the central debate issue.
result_note: Open seat in practice: incumbent Tom Horne (R) lost the primary. Minor candidates (a Green write-in, a No Labels candidate) reported by some sources but unverified.

impact: The governor proposes the state K-12 budget and holds the veto over ESA voucher expansion and school funding formulas, which shape the money available for charter and district programs.
result_note: August polls (HighGround, Noble Predictive) showed Hobbs ahead by roughly 13 to 15 points.

office: Arizona Legislature (all 30 Senate and 60 House seats)
impact: Republicans hold the House 33-27 and Senate 17-13. A Democratic flip of either chamber (first since the 1960s for the House) would change K-12 appropriations and ESA voucher policy.
result_note: Only a handful of districts are competitive; control of both chambers is in play.

office: Arizona statewide propositions touching education (8 legislative referrals)
impact: The ballot includes a school-spending measure (reportedly a classroom or instructional spending requirement, proposition number unverified), Prop 142 (race-based preferences, including in public education) and Prop 318 (school sports by sex at birth). The ESA voucher limit initiative (Prop 212) and its GOP counter (Prop 145) were removed by the Arizona Supreme Court on Aug 18, 2026.
result_note: No ESA voucher measure on the 2026 ballot. Details of the school spending measure unverified.

candidates: Joe Lombardo (R, inc.); Aaron Ford (D); Danielle Ford (I)
impact: Nevada's governor sets the K-12 budget under the Pupil-Centered Funding Plan and has vetoed many Democratic bills; the outcome decides whether Nevada keeps divided government, which affects state money for rural districts like Elko County.
result_note: Toss-up: late-October polling averages roughly tied (about 42 to 44 each). Danielle Ford is a State Board of Education member running nonpartisan/independent.

office: Nevada Legislature (all 42 Assembly seats, 11 of 21 Senate seats)
impact: Democrats hold the Assembly 27-15 and Senate 13-8. A two-thirds supermajority (one more Assembly seat) would let Democrats override vetoes on education funding bills in the 2027 session.
result_note: Democrats favored to keep both chambers; supermajority uncertain.

office: Nevada State Board of Education (elected seats)
impact: Four board members are elected by congressional district and the board helps select the state superintendent; any 2026 seats on the ballot could shift state education policy.
result_note: unverified: could not confirm which seats or candidates are on the 2026 ballot.

office: Nevada statewide ballot questions (Q6 abortion rights, Q7 voter ID)
impact: Only two statewide questions, both second-round constitutional amendments, and neither concerns K-12 funding. A teacher-strike initiative was reported as qualifying but appears not to be on the ballot (unverified).
result_note: No statewide education funding question found.

office: Elko County School District Board of Trustees (nonpartisan)
impact: The trustees approve the district budget and program contracts, including renewal of the Star Academy site.
result_note: Partially verified: Neal and Eden listed for District 1 by GoodParty; filing tracker also lists Jeff Durham (Seat 6) and Brooke Williams Ballard (Seat 7). Incumbent flags unverified. No Elko school bond found.

impact: Booker is a safe-seat Democrat; the seat matters mainly to the national Senate majority that decides Title I and Education Department appropriations.
result_note: Rated Safe D. WHYY reports additional minor-party challengers (names not verified).

impact: Norcross represents Camden, home of Morgan Village Middle School; a safe seat with little direct effect beyond House control.
result_note: Rated Solid D.

impact: Camden's board is an appointed advisory board (members appointed by the mayor; voters kept that in 2018), so there is no Camden school board election. NJ has no governor or legislative race in 2026.
result_note: No election found. Note: Lakeside Middle School exists in Millville (Cumberland Co.) and Pompton Lakes, not Camden; host district unverified.

impact: Republicans hold a narrow majority (about 218-220 seats vs 214-215; Democrats need a net gain of about 3). The House FY27 Labor-HHS-Ed bill cut Title I by nearly $2B (to about $16.5B) and zeroed Title II-A and Title III; a Democratic House would likely block those cuts and Education Department dismantling.
result_note: Exact current seat count varies by source (218-214, 219-215, 220-215) due to vacancies. Democrats modestly favored per August forecasts.

office: US Senate control (35 seats up, including FL and OH specials)
impact: Republicans hold 53-47; Democrats need a net gain of 4. The Senate has resisted House Title I cuts and Congress rejected closing the Education Department in the FY26 law ($79B ED, about $18.4B Title I), so Senate control decides whether FY27 cuts survive.
result_note: Republicans favored to hold per August forecasts. Neither Arizona nor Nevada has a US Senate race in 2026.

impact: Both nominees favor Star's model: Haaland (favored, Solid D) would start career pathways in middle school and expand and stabilize CTE funding, while Hull wants CTE in every district and part of school funding tied to measurable graduation and achievement gains. The governor appoints the PED secretary and sets the budget in a state with roughly 35 percent chronic absenteeism, so either win is an opening for a middle-grades dropout-prevention pitch.
result_note: Haaland is endorsed by AFT New Mexico; Hull is a former Rio Rancho mayor.

office: New Mexico House of Representatives (all 70 seats; Senate not up)
impact: Democrats hold 44 of 70 seats and the chamber is not expected to flip, so the education budget committees that fund CTE and at-risk programs should stay in the same hands. A narrowed margin would matter only if paired with a Hull upset.
result_note: No district-level competitiveness ratings found.

candidates: Frederick Parker (D); John Foreman (R); Jacob Trujillo (D, inc.); Ken Pascoe (R); Sharon Clahchischilliage (R, inc.); Stewart Ingham (R, inc.)
impact: The PEC is split 5-5 and mainly authorizes state charters, so it is only indirectly relevant to a district-partnership vendor like Star. Candidate list and party labels are unverified across sources; District 7 (southern NM, Parker vs Foreman) is the open seat.
result_note: Unverified: full candidate roster by district.

office: Constitutional Amendment 2 (school elections with partisan general elections)
impact: Amendment 2 would let local school board elections share dates with partisan state and federal elections, likely raising turnout and changing board composition. Indirect for Star, since boards approve vendor contracts, but no clear direction.

candidates: Greg Abbott (R, inc.); Gina Hinojosa (D); Pat Dixon (L)
impact: Abbott's priority is the education savings account program, which pulls state dollars toward private and home school rather than district intervention programs; Hinojosa would end ESAs and boost public school funding and revise testing and accountability. A Hinojosa upset would modestly expand district discretionary money, but she would face a Republican Legislature.

office: State Board of Education (8 of 15 seats)
impact: Republicans hold 11 of 15 seats; the SBOE sets curriculum and CTE course standards but not district vendor funding. Indirect for Star.

Franklin (favored) is a former special education teacher and longtime school and CareerTech administrator, a natural ally for a CTE-based at-risk program; Marshall's plan names chronic absenteeism and workforce pathways as targets for regional support zones. Either winner replaces the Walters-era turmoil with a leader receptive to district intervention partnerships.
result_note: Franklin's specific absenteeism or dropout positions not found.

impact: Mazzei (favored) pledges to expand career and technical education pathways with employer partnerships and hire a statewide literacy director; Munson would raise public school investment and end the private-school tax credit. A Mazzei win aligns with Star's career-exploration pitch; a Munson win frees more district dollars.
result_note: Mazzei defeated AG Gentner Drummond in the GOP runoff.

impact: Weiser (favored, CEA-endorsed) backs more K-12 funding via TABOR changes and wants more youth mentorship programs, which fits Star's at-risk intervention model; Marx pledges a spending audit to cut bloat, a headwind for new district contracts.
result_note: Weiser beat Sen. Michael Bennet in the Democratic primary; a third candidate (Lopez) is also on the ballot, party unverified.

office: Proposition NN (keep TABOR excess revenue for K-12)
impact: Proposition NN would let the state retain revenue above the TABOR cap to raise K-12 funding about 2 percent a year for 10 years. Passage would loosen district budgets that are currently too tight for new program purchases like Star.
result_note: Related: Amendment 87 (graduated income tax) and Proposition 136 (income tax cap) also affect revenue.

office: State Board of Education (CD1, CD3, CD7)
candidates: Lisa Escarcega (D, inc.); Frederick Espinoza (R); Sherri Wright (R, inc.); Karla Esser (D, inc.)
impact: Three of nine seats are up; the board oversees accountability and turnaround designations that can drive district demand for intervention programs. Indirect for Star; full candidate list unverified.
result_note: Unverified: Wright's party label and opponents in CD3 and CD7.

office: State Board of Education (8 of 15 seats, partisan)
candidates: LeAnn Wood (R, inc.); Heather Dopp (D); Sarah Reale (D, inc.)
impact: Utah has no governor or superintendent race in 2026; the elected board appoints the state superintendent, so its makeup indirectly shapes openness to outside at-risk programs. Four of eight races were already decided; candidate list unverified.
result_note: Unverified: final ballot lineups and Reale's party label.

impact: Barrera led Thurmond's chronic absenteeism initiative and campaigns on early-warning attendance data, evidence-based attendance strategies, and expanded career pathways, a direct match for Star. Shaw says the state does not need to spend more and should push money to classrooms, more neutral. Note the Legislature has stripped CDE management from the office starting January, reducing its leverage.
result_note: Shaw is Republican-aligned and Barrera Democratic and labor-aligned; office is nonpartisan.

impact: Becerra (favored) has no detailed K-12 plan but backs earlier intervention and tutoring for struggling students and college and career pathways; Hilton would create a voucher-like savings account and eliminate community schools, a headwind for district-run programs.

Kotek's second-term plan targets underperforming K-12 schools with academic performance targets and summer learning; Drazan would reinstate graduation requirements and third-grade retention. Neither names dropout prevention or CTE directly; Oregon has no statewide ballot measures this November.
result_note: Rated Lean D; OEA declined to endorse.

impact: Democrats need about seven House and three to four Senate pickups for a two-thirds supermajority; analysts consider it unlikely this cycle. No governor or superintendent race in 2026, so effects on Star are indirect via budget control.

office: Initiative IL26-001 (parental rights in public schools)
impact: Would undo 2025 legislative changes to the I-2081 parents' rights law; affects school record and notification rules, not program funding. Indirect for Star.

candidates: Debbie Critchfield (R, inc.); Becky Sundin Mitchell (D); Teresa Roundy (other)
impact: Critchfield (favored) built the Idaho Career Ready Students program that expanded CTE statewide and is running on expanding student success pathways, a clear fit for Star's middle-grades career exploration. Her emphasis on local control means pitches go district by district.
result_note: Roundy is the Constitution Party candidate.

impact: Little seeks a third term and is heavily favored; continuity keeps the current workforce and CTE direction in place. Pickens' education agenda not found. Independent and minor-party field unverified.
result_note: Unverified: independent candidates on the general ballot.

office: Montana Legislature (all House, half of Senate)
impact: No governor or superintendent race in 2026. The fate of the 2025 coalition of Democrats and moderate Republicans, which raised school funding and blocked vouchers, hinges on these races after School Freedom Fund-backed conservatives beat several moderates in primaries; a hard-right majority would be a mild headwind for district budgets.

candidates: Eric Barlow (R); Kenneth Casner (D); Rebecca Bextel (other)
impact: Barlow (favored), a state senator, beat Superintendent Megan Degenfelder in the primary; his education agenda was not found in 2026 coverage. Low urgency market for Star.
result_note: Democrat's first name given as Kenneth or Ken; Bextel is Constitution Party.

impact: Harshman (favored), a teacher and the longest-serving House member, leads the Department of Education if elected; his primary platform focused on local control, school choice and testing load rather than dropout prevention. Relationship opportunity but no explicit opening.

candidates: Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D); Bernadette Wilson (R); Dave Bronson (R); Treg Taylor (R)
impact: Kreiss-Tomkins (leading polls, Toss-Up rating) was the only candidate to pledge full education funding, i.e. a higher Base Student Allocation that would give districts room for new programs; a Republican win likely keeps the BSA flat at $6,660. Rural, high-absenteeism districts are a plausible Star fit if funding grows.
result_note: Unverified: Taylor's ballot status after a reported Aug 31 disqualification; he appeared in the Oct 8 debate. Result may take days under ranked-choice tabulation.

impact: Green is a near-certain winner (Solid D); Hawaii runs a single statewide school district under an appointed board, so any Star entry would be a state-level DOE contract. No candidate education agenda relevant to dropout prevention found.

Ramaswamy's platform promotes career-technical education pathways and a results-first, accountability lens on schools, which suits an outcomes-based STEM/career-exploration partnership pitch; Acton would keep the need-based 2022 Fair School Funding formula, sustaining district dollars that can buy intervention programs. Either winner offers an entry point, with Ramaswamy's voucher expansion the main risk to district budgets.
result_note: Open seat (DeWine term-limited). Teachers unions endorsed Acton.

office: State Board of Education (elected district seats)
impact: Ohio's 11 elected board seats are nonpartisan and the board lost most policy authority to the governor-run Department of Education and Workforce in 2023, so these races matter little for Star's entry compared with the governor race.
result_note: Unverified: which districts and candidates are on the 2026 ballot could not be confirmed from 2026 sources. Only statewide issue is Issue 3 (voter ID), not education.

impact: John James pledges that every non-college-bound student will graduate with a trade certification, license, or career-ready portfolio and wants governor control of the state superintendent, a direct opening for a middle-grades career-exploration pipeline; Benson's weighted (need-based) funding formula would steer more money to high-poverty districts that buy at-risk programs. Benson led late polling by about 6 to 7 points.
result_note: Open seat (Whitmer term-limited). Mike Duggan dropped his independent bid in May 2026.

office: State Board of Education (2 at-large seats)
candidates: Judith Pritchett (D); Tiffany Tilley (D, inc.); Terence Collins (R); Bree Moeggenberg (R)
impact: Two of eight seats are up on a board that is 6-2 Democratic, so control will not flip, but the board hires the state superintendent and sets policy on accountability and intervention; relevant mainly if James wins and pushes to strip its authority.
result_note: Incumbency of Tilley assumed from her current board service; Pritchett incumbency not confirmed.

office: State House and State Senate control
candidates: Michigan House Republicans (58-52 majority) (R, inc.); Michigan Senate Democrats (narrow majority) (D, inc.)
impact: Both chambers are in play (Democrats need about four House seats; the Senate is a one or two seat Democratic edge), so the result decides whether the next governor gets a trifecta to pass a new funding formula or a CTE mandate that could carry dedicated at-risk dollars.
result_note: Senate seat counts differ across sources (19-18 vs 20-18).

candidates: Indiana House Republicans (70-30) (R, inc.); Indiana House Democrats (D)
impact: No governor or state superintendent race in 2026 (the schools chief is now an appointed secretary of education under Gov. Mike Braun). Democrats need four House seats to break the GOP two-thirds supermajority; Republican control is not at risk, so Star's path runs through the Braun administration regardless.
result_note: Trump-backed challengers ousted several GOP senators in May primaries; Senate GOP leadership change underway.

candidates: JB Pritzker (D, inc.); Darren Bailey (R); Collin Corbett (I)
impact: A Pritzker third term keeps growing evidence-based funding that flows most to high-need districts, giving them discretionary money for intervention vendors; Bailey argues schools need less government, not more funding, which would tighten district budgets. Pritzker is favored in this rematch.
result_note: Rematch of 2022; IEA endorsed Pritzker.

impact: Crowley promises reliable, increased K-12 funding and expanded career readiness programs linking students to apprenticeships and technical schools, an opening for a career-exploration feeder program; Tiffany would add A-F school grades and accountability for struggling districts, which could also create demand for turnaround partners but with voucher-friendly budgets.
result_note: Open seat (Evers retiring).

candidates: Wisconsin Senate Republicans (18-15) (R, inc.); Wisconsin Assembly Republicans (54-45) (R, inc.)
impact: Democrats need two Senate seats (rated lean D) and five Assembly seats to flip; a Crowley trifecta would make large K-12 funding increases and career-readiness grants far more likely than under divided government.

Klobuchar's plan has the state partner with schools on tutoring, daily attendance tracking and required meetings for students who fall behind, framed inside a workforce plan that doubles apprenticeships; that is a near-exact match for Star's chronic-absenteeism and at-risk intervention model. Demuth focuses on performance pay, mandate opt-outs and private-school safety funding.
result_note: Open seat (Walz not running). DFL favored in polling.

candidates: Minnesota House (tied 67-67) (other, inc.); Minnesota Senate DFL (34-33) (D, inc.)
impact: Both chambers are effectively tied; whichever party wins likely holds power until 2030, deciding whether Klobuchar's attendance and tutoring initiatives get funded or stall in divided government.

Sand pledges to fully fund public schools, frames an 'educational crisis' tied to a 'workforce crisis', and wants tighter voucher oversight, which would ease district budget pressure from the ESA program; Lahn's education platform was not found. Markets favored Sand heavily.
result_note: Open seat (Reynolds retiring). Lahn education positions unverified.

candidates: Iowa House Republicans (67-33) (R, inc.); Iowa Senate Republicans (33-17) (R, inc.)
impact: Republicans hold exactly two-thirds of the House and lost the Senate supermajority in 2025; a Sand win paired with GOP loss of supermajorities would give him veto leverage over education budgets.

The school finance formula expires at the end of 2026, so the winner shapes the next one: Holscher would only sign a formula that fully funds schools and special education, freeing district money; Masterson wants a Mississippi-style literacy push, tax-credit scholarships and scrutiny of what taxpayers get, plus a 3% property valuation cap that could squeeze local discretionary budgets.
result_note: Open seat (Kelly term-limited).

office: State Board of Education (5 open seats: Districts 1, 3, 5, 7, 9)
candidates: Jim McMullen (D3) (R); Amy Diediker (D3) (D); Jean Clifford (D5) (R); Destry Brown (D9) (R)
impact: All five seats are open after GOP incumbents retired and most holdover members are Democrats, so the elected board's Republican majority could flip; the board sets accreditation and CTE pathway policy that affects how districts justify career-exploration programs.
result_note: Unverified: full matchups for Districts 1, 5, 7 and 9 (Democratic opponents) not confirmed; District numbers other than 3, 5 and 9 assumed.

impact: Walz, a former teacher and Education Committee chair, wants high schools to offer individualized paths such as career and technical education (citing Fremont as a model), an opening for Star; Pillen favors school choice (Opportunity Scholarships) and property-tax-driven funding changes. Race is close with Pillen slightly ahead.

office: State Board of Education (4 district seats)
candidates: Elizabeth Tegtmeier (D7) (NP, inc.); Sherry Jones (D6) (NP, inc.); Grady Erickson (D6) (NP); Lana Daws / Angie Eberspacher / Michaela Conway (D5, two advanced) (NP)
impact: The nonpartisan board is split 4-4 by party affiliation, so the competitive District 5 race could tip its majority; indirect effect on Star via state CTE and accountability rules.
result_note: Unverified: which two District 5 candidates advanced and the District 8 field were not confirmed.

impact: Republicans hold exactly the 33 seats needed to break filibusters; May primary results suggest they could lose it, which would limit further school-choice and funding-formula changes.

Rhoden, heavily favored after winning the July 28 runoff 71-29 over Toby Doeden, backs Education Savings Accounts and opted into federal school choice, with no stated dropout or CTE initiative; Ahlers says property tax changes must not short schools. Star would need to sell directly to districts and the appointed education secretary.
result_note: No education measure on SD's statewide ballot.

impact: The elected chief directly runs DPI; appointed incumbent Bachmeier (former West Fargo business manager) runs on improving student outcomes and readiness for college, career and military, while Foss, backed by the Democratic-NPL, is a former CTE leader who teaches technology and engineering at a Grand Forks middle school, the closest possible fit to Star's model. Bachmeier is favored after taking 56% in the June primary.
result_note: No governor race in ND in 2026.

office: Initiated constitutional measure: universal free school breakfast and lunch
impact: Passage would add a constitutional spending mandate on the K-12 budget that could compete with discretionary program dollars, though it also signals voter appetite for whole-child supports.
result_note: Measure numbering differs across sources; a separate 60% amendment-threshold measure is also on the ballot.

impact: Woods, a three-term incumbent who survived a June runoff against Fred Longgrear, touts a graduation rate rising from 70% to 85.4% and 98%+ graduation for CTE pathway completers, making a middle-grades career-exploration and dropout-prevention pitch a natural fit with GaDOE. Powell attacks $100M in voucher spending and wants more invested in public schools, which also favors district-side program purchases, so either winner gives Star an opening; Woods offers continuity with an existing CTE frame.
result_note: Woods won the GOP nomination in the June 16, 2026 runoff over Fred Longgrear.

impact: Jackson (who beat Lt. Gov. Burt Jones in the GOP runoff) wants to teach more high schoolers trades such as plumbing, electrical and HVAC and introduce engineering and technical jobs earlier in school, which aligns directly with Star's middle-school STEM and career-exploration model. Bottoms backs free technical college and fully funding education; a Jackson win is the stronger opening for workforce-framed K-12 grants.
result_note: Open seat (Kemp term-limited).

impact: Donalds's Student Success Plan would require a personalized academic and career roadmap for every public school student by sixth grade, with workforce and trade paths equally resourced and industry partners designing career tracks, an almost exact match for Star's middle-grades career-exploration model. Jolly (FEA-endorsed) calls public education in crisis and wants more investment, a softer but still positive environment; a Donalds win is the clearest opening.
result_note: Open seat (DeSantis term-limited); Donalds favored in ratings and markets.

impact: Raises the non-school homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 and needs 60% to pass; school district levies are largely insulated, so district budgets for programs like Star are not directly cut, but county and city revenue losses could squeeze local co-funded youth and workforce programs.

office: NC General Assembly: House veto-proof supermajority
impact: Republicans hold 71 of 120 House seats, one short of the 72 needed to override Gov. Stein without Democratic help (the Senate already has 30 of 50). A GOP pickup would let the legislature override on school-choice and spending bills that steer state dollars away from district discretionary budgets; a Democratic hold keeps Stein's veto as leverage for district-focused funding. No governor or superintendent race in 2026, so the legislature is the main lever.

office: Constitutional amendments: 3.5% income tax cap and local property tax limits
impact: Capping the state income tax at 3.5% (down from a 7% ceiling) and limiting local property tax increases would constrain long-run state and county revenue for K-12, making new district contracts for outside programs harder to fund. Polling shows roughly two-thirds support for each.

office: Kentucky General Assembly (all 100 House, 19 of 38 Senate seats)
impact: Republican supermajorities (80-20 House, 32-6 Senate) are not seriously at risk, with many seats uncontested, so the legislature keeps control of SEEK and discretionary education appropriations heading into the 2027 governor race. Watch for any budget language on at-risk or workforce grants rather than a change in control.

Lt. Gov. Coleman, a former teacher and assistant principal who founded the Lead Kentucky education nonprofit, has made public schools her calling card and campaigned against diverting public funds outside public education, favoring district-level partnerships like Star. Adkins is a former Beshear senior adviser. Republican field unverified (Comer, Adams, Thayer rumored but undeclared); May 18, 2027 primary.
result_note: Republican candidates unverified; no major Republican had declared in sources found.

office: Constitutional amendments (reproductive freedom, marriage, voting rights restoration)
impact: None of Virginia's three November 2026 amendments touches education funding; no governor race until 2029 (Spanberger elected 2025). Little direct effect on Star's entry.

office: Virginia General Assembly (all 40 Senate and 100 House seats)
impact: The 2027 legislative elections will decide whether Democrats keep the trifecta behind the Standards of Quality funding and any new at-risk or CTE add-ons a Star pitch would rely on. Candidates unverified.
result_note: Candidates unverified; 2027 race.

impact: Moore is heavily favored in a 2022 rematch; he has promised to fully fund the Blueprint for Maryland's Future (which includes college and career readiness pathways) but proposed trimming Blueprint growth in 2025, so new money is tight. A Moore win means continuity and a Blueprint-aligned career-readiness pitch; a Cox upset would be unpredictable for district discretionary spending.

No governor race or statewide measures in 2026; Democrats hold 15-6 Senate and 27-14 House supermajorities and would lose them with a three-seat Republican gain in either chamber. Control is not at risk, so education budget direction stays with Gov. Meyer and Democratic leaders.

Lewis George, the presumptive winner of the open seat (Bowser not running), wants to expand vocational, technical and career-focused programs and fund supports so students stay in school, and could install a new deputy mayor for education and DCPS chancellor. New leadership plus a career-pathways agenda creates an entry point for a pitch to DCPS and charter LEAs.
result_note: Independent candidates on the ballot not fully verified.

candidates: Eric Goulet (Ward 3) (NP); Joshua Wiley (Ward 6) (NP); Jon Alfuth (Ward 5) (NP)
impact: The SBOE sets standards and graduation requirements but does not control spending; new members could shape attendance and career-readiness policy. Candidate roster incomplete and unverified.
result_note: Candidate list unverified and incomplete.

impact: Shapiro (up 59-34 in an October Quinnipiac poll) has raised CTE and apprenticeship funding nearly 50%, proposed another $18M plus doubling Schools-to-Work funding, and added over $3B in K-12 adequacy funding to underfunded districts, giving districts both money and a workforce frame for Star. Garrity wants to fund students and outcomes rather than systems, which could also support outcomes-based contracts.

office: Pennsylvania State Senate control (25 of 50 seats)
impact: Republicans hold the Senate 27-23 and Sabato rates it a toss-up; a Democratic net gain of three seats would give Shapiro a trifecta (House is 103-100 D) and make further adequacy and CTE dollars to high-need districts easier to pass.

Hochul leads Blakeman by double digits; a Hochul win means continuity in Foundation Aid-driven district budgets, where Star would sell to districts using existing aid. No explicit dropout-prevention or middle-grades CTE plank found from either candidate.

Lamont is favored for a third term; Fazio's campaign centers on energy costs and the largest middle-class tax cut in state history, which could pressure education spending if he won. No education-specific opening identified from either.

candidates: Helena Foulkes (D); Aaron Guckian or Elaine Pelino (unverified) (R); Ken Block (I); Jay Gotra (I); C.D. Reynolds (I)
impact: Foulkes, who ousted Gov. McKee in the September primary, calls RI's education system broken and has tied her tenure to student outcomes; her plan adds K-8 teaching assistants and school mental health staff and proposes a $100M bond for classroom-to-career facilities. A Foulkes win creates an outcomes-focused state leader with a career-pathways budget line Star can align with.
result_note: Republican nominee unverified: Guckian vs Pelino primary was close with a recount requested.

impact: Healey is strongly favored; none of the nine statewide ballot questions addresses K-12 funding. Continuity means Star would enter through district Chapter 70 and existing state grant programs rather than a new state initiative.
Scott is favored for a sixth term; Vermont's small, rural districts and ongoing focus on property-tax-driven education costs limit near-term appetite for new outside programs regardless of winner.

candidates: Kelly Ayotte (R, inc.); Cinde Warmington (D); Stephen Villee (L)
impact: Ayotte, the favorite, signed universal Education Freedom Accounts and budgets about $50M for them, steering new money toward families rather than district programs; Warmington pledges to repeal EFAs, which would keep more state dollars in district budgets. Neither has a dropout-prevention or middle-grades CTE agenda.

candidates: Hannah Pingree (D); Bobby Charles (R); Rick Bennett (I)
impact: Open seat (Mills term-limited); Pingree leads and says schools need a shakeup, focusing on teacher shortages, early childhood and school-based mental health, while Charles criticizes falling outcomes. An outcomes-focused new administration could be receptive, but no explicit dropout-prevention or CTE plank was found.
